title: Tier II Checkpoint II — An Integrated Project

pts: Set a substantial, learner-driven outcome running across several weeks, with genuine learner choice built into it.
Map the project's stages — planning, research, production, presentation — onto the scheme of work explicitly.
Build in interim checkpoints along the way, not just a single final deadline.

v: Scheme of work (Unit 14); project planning grid (Unit 36)

items: Write the project’s final outcome in one sentence, naming a real audience.
List the four stages: planning, research, production, presentation.
Place the stages on the scheme of work, week by week, alongside required coursebook units.
Build in learner choice: at least two options for topic focus or product type.
Add two interim checkpoints with a small, visible output at each.
Show the frame to the class and let groups propose the options.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Outcome: Groups recommend one water-saving measure for the school to the headteacher and the School Management Committee (SMC), in a short presentation and a one-page proposal.
Week 1: planning and water audit of the school. Week 2: research (texts, interviews, data). Week 3: simulation, debate and drafting. Week 4: practice run, final presentations, reflection.
Choice: groups choose a focus (tap leaks, rainwater harvesting, garden watering, awareness among younger classes) and a product (poster campaign, leaflet or short video).
Checkpoint 1 (end of week 1): audit sheet. Checkpoint 2 (end of week 3): proposal draft.

blocks.x: This applies Unit 36 directly: a substantial, learner-driven outcome with interim checkpoints rather than one final deadline.

body: Purpose: to show stages and checkpoints. Content: a road across four weeks with milestones ‘plan’, ‘research’, ‘produce’, ‘present’, two flags for checkpoints, and a school with an audience waiting at the end. Style: map-like, cheerful. Board version: a line with four marks and two flags.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a week-by-week project grid.

blocks.x: The project road drawn on chart paper and displayed on the wall.

pts: Ask whether the project could integrate real subject content, even lightly, raising its cognitive and communicative authenticity.
Where it does, plan support for both content and language demands using the 4Cs framework as a lens.
This isn't required for every project, but worth deliberately considering rather than defaulting against.

v: Teacher activity; B1 learners for the audit
Science and geography textbooks for the same class; a 4Cs planning sheet (Unit 37)

items: Check what the science and social science syllabus says about water for this class.
Decide whether one or two content elements could feed the project.
Complete a 4Cs sheet: content, communication, cognition, culture.
Identify the language of learning (key terms), language for learning (functions for the task) and language through learning (what emerges).
Agree a shared lesson or resource with the subject teacher.
If there is no natural content link, note why and move on; not every project needs one.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Content: the water cycle; rainwater harvesting; reading a rainfall bar chart.
Communication: describing a process (first, then, as a result); comparing quantities (more than, twice as much); making recommendations (we recommend that…).
Cognition: interpreting data; evaluating options; justifying a choice.
Culture: traditional water-saving practices in the learners’ communities, such as stepwells and temple tanks.

blocks.x: Coyle, Hood and Marsh (2010) present the 4Cs as a planning lens, not a checklist to complete for its own sake.

body: Purpose: to show the 4Cs applied to one topic. Content: a square window with four panes, each showing one C: a water-cycle diagram (content), two learners talking (communication), a thinking learner with a bar chart (cognition), and a stepwell (culture). Style: clean, illustrative. Board version: a square divided into four with one word in each.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared 4Cs sheet with the subject teacher.

blocks.x: A 4Cs sheet in the planning notebook, shared at a staffroom meeting.

pts: Consider whether part of the project could take the form of a role-play or simulation — a mock client meeting, a simulated negotiation.
This raises communicative pressure and genre authenticity at a natural point within the project's arc.
Debrief any role-play or simulation stage explicitly, connecting performance back to the project's real outcome.

items: Set the scene: a simulated SMC meeting to discuss the school’s water problem.
Give each learner in a group of six a role card: headteacher, parent member, SMC chair, school cleaner, learner representative, local councillor.
Allow five minutes to prepare, using the role card and the week 2 research.
Groups hold the meeting and agree two options to take to the debate.
Debrief: what did each role care about, and what language worked to persuade?
Invite an SMC member or parent to observe one group.
Support: role cards with key phrases and home-language notes.
Challenge: role cards with a hidden concern that must emerge during the meeting.

blocks.x: A role card (written for this book):

lines: Parent member. You worry that children do not have enough drinking water in the afternoon. You support any plan that is cheap and quick.
In my opinion, the first priority should be…
I understand your point, but…
Could we agree to look into…?
A: As the cleaner, I can tell you that three taps near the toilets leak all day.
B: Then could we agree to report them this week?

blocks.x: This applies Unit 38 and Jones’s (1982) view of simulation as real function in a simulated setting: it raises communicative pressure at a natural point, and the debrief links performance to the real outcome.

body: Purpose: to show a simulation within a project. Content: six learners around benches with name tents (‘Headteacher’, ‘Parent’, ‘Cleaner’ and so on), a water jug and an agenda on the board. Style: lively, classroom-real. Board version: a rectangle with six labelled positions.

items: None needed; role cards are printed or handwritten.

blocks.x: Handwritten role cards and name tents made from folded paper.

pts: Where the project involves decision-making, structure it with assigned positions and argument criteria, not open discussion alone.
This distributes participation fairly across the project group, echoing Unit 39's core rationale.
Note recurring argumentative-language gaps for a language-focus session partway through the project.

v: Position cards; argument criteria (Unit 39); a language-gap notebook

items: Assign each pair within a group one of the two options to argue, regardless of preference.
Share the argument criteria: a clear claim, a reason, evidence from research, a response to the other side.
Pairs argue for three minutes each; the group then questions both sides.
The group decides which measure to recommend, giving reasons.
While groups debate, note recurring language gaps for a short language-focus session in the following lesson.
A ‘fishbowl’: one group debates while the rest assess against the criteria.
Support: argument frames on the board.
Challenge: learners must quote a number or fact from a source in every turn.

lines: We believe the school should… because…
According to the rainfall data, …
Our opponents say…, but…

blocks.x: Language gaps the teacher noted in the worked project:

lines: Comparatives with quantities: ‘more cheaper’, ‘less litres’.
Hedging: learners said ‘It will save all the water’ rather than ‘It could save a lot of water’.

blocks.x: The next lesson opens with ten minutes on fewer/less and could/might. Assigned positions distribute participation fairly (Unit 39).

body: Purpose: to show structured debate within a project. Content: a large tap in the centre; on one side, a pair of learners with a card ‘Fix the leaks’; on the other, a pair with ‘Harvest the rain’; small speech bubbles show claims and evidence. Style: balanced, clear. Board version: a T-chart with two headings.

items: A phone timer (free) for strict turn lengths.

blocks.x: A sand timer or the wall clock.

pts: Give the project a genuine presentation stage, scaffolded appropriately to the group's level.
Build in low-stakes practice runs before the final presentation, protecting learners from unmanaged anxiety.
Use structured peer feedback criteria for the practice run, connecting to Unit 43's collaborative-assessment principles.

items: Each group gives a three-minute practice presentation to one other group, not to the whole class.
The listening group uses a three-question checklist and writes one star and one step.
Groups swap roles.
Each group chooses two changes to make before the final presentation.
Final presentations are given to the class, with the headteacher or an SMC member invited if possible.
Groups record the practice run on a phone and review it first.
Support: a presentation frame with an opening, three points and a closing request.
Challenge: groups prepare for two likely questions from the audience.

lines: Is the recommendation clear in the first thirty seconds?
Is there one piece of evidence for each reason?
Does every member of the group speak?

blocks.x: Peer feedback from the worked project:

lines: Star: Your bar chart showed the rainfall clearly.
Step: Say your recommendation at the start, not only at the end.

blocks.x: A low-stakes practice run protects learners from unmanaged anxiety (Unit 22) and gives peer feedback a clear purpose: revision (Topping 1998).

body: Purpose: to show a practice run as a protected stage. Content: two small groups facing each other across a bench, one presenting, one holding feedback slips; behind them an empty stage labelled ‘Friday’. Style: calm, encouraging. Board version: two small circles facing each other.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for groups with access to design slides or posters.

blocks.x: Chart-paper posters and handwritten cue cards.

body: Invite the real audience in week 1. A headteacher or SMC member asked early is more likely to attend, and learners take a task more seriously when the audience is real.

pts: Ground the project's research stage in authentic materials, graded by task rather than simplified as texts.
Draw on the authentic-materials bank suggested in Unit 41, if one has been built, rather than starting from scratch each time.
This raises the real-world resemblance of both the process and the final outcome.

v: A pack of five authentic texts; task cards graded by level

items: Assemble a pack from the staffroom text bank (Unit 41), adding one or two new items.
For each text, write two or three task cards at different levels of demand.
Groups choose the texts relevant to their focus and a task card suited to them.
Groups record key facts on a shared research sheet, with the source of each fact.
Groups add a text they find themselves, such as a notice from home.
Support: the easiest task card for each text; a glossary strip.
Challenge: the hardest task card, requiring comparison of two sources.

blocks.x: The worked project’s pack (types of text; use current local examples):

lines: a municipal notice about water supply timings;
a newspaper report on groundwater levels in the district;
a leaflet on rooftop rainwater harvesting;
a bar chart of monthly rainfall;
a short radio or podcast interview with a farmer about borewells.
Easier: Find the days and times water is supplied.
Harder: What problem does this notice suggest? What could the school do about it?

blocks.x: The texts are not simplified; the tasks are graded, and starting from the bank saves time.

body: Purpose: to show research from authentic materials. Content: a group at a bench covered with a newspaper cutting, a leaflet, a notice and a chart; one learner fills in a ‘fact’ and ‘source’ sheet. Style: realistic, busy but clear. Board version: a two-column table.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a shared digital text pack.

blocks.x: Photocopied or cut-out texts in a labelled envelope per group.

pts: Have learners maintain a brief reflective log across the project's stages, not just submit a single final product.
This distributes assessment weight across the project's development, consistent with Unit 42's portfolio principles.
Combine this with product and presentation assessment for a full, multi-dimensional picture of the outcome.

v: 5 minutes at the end of each project lesson; 30 minutes for final assessment
A log page in the portfolio (Unit 42); an assessment grid

items: Each learner keeps a log page with one entry per project lesson.
Each entry answers two prompts: What did I do today? What did I learn or find difficult?
At the end, learners choose two entries that show their development and add a short reflection.
Assess three elements: the log and reflection, the group product, and the presentation.
Combine with contribution evidence (Unit 43) for an individual mark.
Learners may write log entries in the home language in week 1, moving to English as the project progresses.
Support: a word bank for reflection.
Challenge: a final reflection comparing the first and last weeks.

lines: Week 1: I counted taps with Farhan. We found eleven. Three were leaking. I did not know the word ‘leak’ before.
Week 3: In the debate I used ‘according to the chart’. I felt more confident.
Log and reflection 30%, group product 35%, presentation 35%, adjusted for individual contribution.

blocks.x: This spreads assessment across the project’s development (Unit 42) and involves learners in judging their own progress (Little 2005).

body: Purpose: to show multi-dimensional assessment. Content: a project folder in the centre with three spotlights shining on it, labelled ‘log’, ‘product’ and ‘presentation’; small percentages on each beam. Style: clear, even-handed. Board version: a rectangle with three lines drawn to it.

items: Google Sheets (free) for the assessment grid.

blocks.x: The log page in the paper portfolio and a grid in the teacher’s record book.

pts: Build in structured peer feedback at a key interim stage, using clear, specific criteria.
Consider which project stages could move outside class time, protecting in-class time for interaction and negotiation.
This closes the loop on this stretch of Tier II — the same integration principles, now at full project scale.

v: The complete project plan; an access map (Unit 44)

items: Mark the stage where structured peer feedback will happen (in the worked example, the proposal draft in week 3).
Mark stages that could move outside class: reading, interviews at home, drafting.
Check each outside stage against the access map and add an offline route.
Confirm that in-class time is protected for the simulation, the debate and the presentations.
Using the worked example as a model, draft the frame for your own project with your own class.
Swap plans with a colleague for peer feedback, using this unit’s eight points as criteria.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Outside class: reading the text pack; interviewing a family member about water use (in any language, with three notes in English); drafting the proposal.
In class: the SMC simulation; the debate; peer feedback on drafts; practice runs; final presentations.
Offline routes: printed texts go home in envelopes; learners without phones take interview notes on paper.

blocks.x: A planning checklist for your own project:

lines: Outcome and audience? Stages and checkpoints? Content angle? Simulation? Debate? Presentation with practice run? Authentic texts? Log? Peer feedback? Outside-class stages with offline routes?

blocks.x: The same integration principles that shaped one lesson in Unit 35 now shape four weeks of work.

body: Purpose: to close this stretch of Part II. Content: a cloth woven from nine coloured threads labelled Units 36 to 44, forming a water drop in the centre. Style: rich, textile-like. Board version: nine lines crossing into a simple grid.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shareable project plan template.

blocks.x: A one-page project plan in the planning notebook.

body: Take the planning checklist from this point and use it to audit a project you have already run. Mark each item as present, partly present or absent. Add the most important missing item to your next project.

dek: Unit 45 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier II by designing one full project end-to-end, showing where Units 36 through 44 meet in a single piece of real planning.

aims.x: Unit 35 showed that a single lesson could integrate the foundations of Part II. This checkpoint does the same at project scale. It follows one worked example from first idea to final assessment: a four-week project for a Class 9 group of 48 learners at around B1, called ‘Every Drop Counts: Saving Water in Our School’. Each point applies one of Units 36–44 to that project, so that you can see where they meet in a single piece of real planning, and then plan a project of your own.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: frame a multi-week project with stages, choice and interim checkpoints;
decide whether and how to add a content angle using the 4Cs;
place a role-play or simulation at a natural point in a project;
structure a decision-making stage as a debate with assigned positions;
plan a scaffolded presentation stage with a practice run and peer feedback;
ground a project’s research stage in authentic materials graded by task;
assess a project through a reflective log, the product and the presentation together;
decide which project stages can move outside class, fairly and with offline routes.

why: Why this matters. Checkpoint I proved a single integrated lesson could combine this tier's foundations. This checkpoint proves the same at project scale, before the tier's final stretch.

background.x: Legutke and Thomas (1991) described projects as a way of making the classroom a place of genuine experience and shared decision-making, and Fried-Booth (2002) set out a practical sequence from planning through research to a product. Beckett and Miller’s (2006) collection shows that projects can integrate language, content and skills, but also that they need structure if language development is not to be lost in the busy work of making things. Units 36–44 took the elements one at a time: projects, content, role-play, debate, presentations, authentic materials, portfolios, peer feedback and blended design.

A checkpoint adds nothing new; it tests whether those elements can work together in an ordinary Indian classroom. The worked project assumes realistic constraints: fixed benches, 48 learners, four English periods a week of 40 minutes, one shared projector, and mixed home access to phones. It uses a topic that crosses subjects and connects with learners’ lives, as the NEP 2020 asks with its call for experiential, integrated and inquiry-based learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) and the NCF 2023 with its emphasis on learners’ surroundings (NCERT 2023). Learners in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu or Rajasthan know about tankers, borewells and monsoon rains from experience, often through conversations at home in Kannada, Tamil, Marwari or Urdu.
Follow the worked example point by point, then use the planning activities to design your own project. The decisions will differ; the questions will be the same.

items: Project plan. Assess a teacher’s own project plan against the eight points of this unit, with peer feedback from a colleague.
Learner outcomes. Assess logs, products and presentations with shared criteria, adjusted for individual contribution.
Language focus. Check whether the language gaps noted during the debate improve in the final presentations and proposals.
Learner voice. Ask: ‘What did you learn from this project that you could not learn from the textbook alone?’
Which of Units 36–44 do you already use confidently, and which have you not yet tried?
What real audience could your learners address with a project?
Where could a content link with another subject strengthen a project in your school?
Which stages of a project could your learners manage outside class, and which need you?
How would you adapt the worked project for a class at A2, or for a class with no access to phones?
What would convince a sceptical colleague or headteacher that project time is well spent?

perm: Newspaper articles, notices and leaflets used in class should follow the copyright guidance in Unit 41; the book itself describes text types rather than reproducing specific published items.

The worked project, role cards, task cards, logs and plans are original and written for this book. Authentic texts used in class (notices, newspaper reports, leaflets, charts, interviews) should be used within copyright guidance or replaced with original equivalents in the book. Screenshots of Google Sheets, Docs, Padlet or Canva require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: A planning framework for CLIL that asks teachers to integrate content, communication, cognition and culture in each unit (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010); for example, a science lesson on the water cycle also plans its language and thinking demands.

In a debate or discussion, a viewpoint that a learner is given to argue rather than one they personally hold; it separates the argument from the arguer and lowers the emotional stakes of disagreement.
A collection of short real-world texts, such as newspaper extracts, notices and reports, assembled to support the research stage of a project or simulation.
An extended project, over several weeks, that combines skills and stages such as research, simulation, debate and presentation to produce a real outcome for a real audience.
A planned point during a project where learners produce a small, visible output, so that the teacher can check progress and give feedback before the final product.
A stage of a project or unit that learners carry out beyond the classroom, such as interviewing people or gathering information, ideally with an offline route for learners without devices.
A rehearsal of a presentation or performance before the real event, often with peer feedback, to build confidence and improve delivery.
A record kept by learners during a project, noting what they did, what they learnt and what they will do next, often used in assessment.

People beyond the teacher who will genuinely read, hear or use learners’ work, such as parents, a headteacher, SMC members or another class. Writing or presenting for a real audience raises motivation and makes the task more purposeful.

An extended activity in which learners act within a realistic, structured situation, such as a village panchayat meeting or a news studio, often keeping their own views and drawing on information provided.
